newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Gulf Canada wins Clyde by a whisker.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Gulf Canada wins Clyde by a whisker.

text.p: Gulf Canada Resources Ltd emerged triumphant on Tuesday from one of the most bitter bid battles in the oil exploration industry in recent years when it won control of Clyde Petroleum Plc by a whisker.
The Canadian firm said it held 51.42 percent of Clyde Petroleum shares after its 494 million pound ($793 million) hostile offer closed at 1300 GMT.
"Obviously, given that control of our company has passed by the finest of margins, we are extremely disappointed by the outcome," said Clyde chairman Malcolm Gourlay.
Clyde had argued that Gulf Canada's offer was too low as it ignored growth prospects.
The acquisition of Clyde gives Gulf Canada a firm base in the North Sea, exposure to Australia and a bigger presence in Indonesia, which was already one of its core areas.
The Canadian company's bid was the latest in a wave of takeovers in the oil exploration and production (E&P) sector since late 1995. More acquisition activity could be expected, analysts said.
After years of cost-cutting to fight depressed oil prices, many oil firms are awash with cash for acquisitions to replace or expand oil and gas reserves.
A prolonged rally which in late 1996 took oil prices to their highest levels since the 1990-1991 Gulf War has also made E&P stocks attractive.
"I wouldn't be surprised to see one more (bid) before the year," said one analyst. "People have the cash and the sector is much better managed. There are some incredible targets out there."

But the Clyde takeover showed the E&P industry was unwilling to pay over the odds after the sector suffered from a sharp stock market decline in the early 1990s following a period of bid-inflated speculation, analysts said.

Gulf Canada originally offered 105 pence per share, which was widely considered too low. The company, headed by tough-talking Texas oilman J.P. Bryan, was forced to raise its offer to 120 pence amid persistent speculation that rivals were poised to launch counter bids.
Nevertheless, analysts said Gulf Canada showed restraint since some wondered whether the 120 pence offer would be successful.
"It was reasonable value. It certainly wasn't a massive premium over what people think is fair value," said one industry-watcher.
Investors may have had second thoughts about accepting the offer but later relented amid fears that Clyde's shares would fall drastically if the bid failed, analysts said.
Clyde shares traded at 84-1/2 pence just before Gulf Canada first expressed its takeover interest in mid-December. ($1=.6227 Pound)
